bib.title: Accelerated Hierarchical Density Clustering
bib.venue: preprint (arXiv v2, May 2017); published ICDM Workshops 2017 per DOI

question: Can HDBSCAN* be computed with sub-quadratic, near N log N average-case run-time so it matches DBSCAN's speed while keeping variable-density clusters and no epsilon parameter?
hypothesis: Replacing the O(N^2) steps (core distances, MST) with space-tree nearest-neighbour search and a Dual-Tree Boruvka MST makes HDBSCAN* scale comparably to DBSCAN.
contributions: Three descriptions of HDBSCAN* (statistical, DBSCAN*-based computational, topological/sheaf); the topological one is claimed as new
Accelerated HDBSCAN* using kd-/ball-tree core distances and a Dual-Tree Boruvka MST adapted to mutual reachability distance
Run-time scaling benchmarks against the Java reference HDBSCAN*, eight scikit-learn algorithms and DBSCAN

method.summary: Core distances come from kd-tree or ball-tree k-nearest-neighbour queries; the MST of the mutual reachability graph comes from a Dual-Tree Boruvka algorithm (March et al. 2010, in the Curtin et al. 2013 framework) with core-distance filtering and tie handling that gives an approximate MST; then sort edges, union-find single linkage tree, condensed tree and stability-based flat extraction. Implemented in Python on scikit-learn and benchmarked for run-time only.

results.claim: Accelerated Python HDBSCAN* is about two orders of magnitude faster than the Java reference at 200,000 points, in both 2-d and 50-d.
results.setup: Synthetic 2-d and 50-d data, Python accelerated vs Java reference, MacBook Pro 3.1 GHz i7 8GB
results.quote: the accelerated Python version demonstrates roughly two orders of magnitude better absolute run-time performance on data set sizes of 200,000 points
results.note: Read from Fig 4 narrative; the baseline implementation is in a different language, so part of the gap is implementation

results.claim: On scikit-learn defaults, K-Means, DBSCAN and HDBSCAN* form the fastest group and are hard to tell apart; Affinity Propagation, Spectral Clustering and Mean Shift degrade beyond a few thousand points.
results.setup: Default parameters, scikit-learn v0.18.1, Fig 5 and 6
results.quote: DBSCAN, K-Means and HDBSCAN*, which are difficult to tell apart from one another

results.claim: Accelerated HDBSCAN* shows comparable asymptotic and absolute run-time to scikit-learn DBSCAN across dimensions and cluster counts, with DBSCAN parameters tuned to match HDBSCAN* output.
results.n: ten random data sets per parameter combination
results.setup: Gaussian-ball mixtures, Fig 7; DBSCAN epsilon and k found by Gaussian-process search maximising adjusted Rand index
results.quote: our accelerated algorithm has comparable asymptotic performance to DBSCAN
results.note: Authors concede that in 2-d overlapping Gaussians give variable-density output DBSCAN cannot reproduce, so 2-d DBSCAN timings are uncertain

results.claim: The original HDBSCAN* has O(N^2) run-time; the accelerated version is argued to approach O(N log N) on average, with no strict bound given.
results.setup: Depends on data distribution and space tree (kd-tree, ball-tree)
results.quote: we can certainly approach O(N log N) asymptotic performance for many data sets

limits: Run-time only; clustering quality is explicitly not evaluated (deferred to Campello et al. 2013, 2015).
Benchmarks use synthetic Gaussian mixtures; real data and noisy background left as an extension.
Different-language reference comparison conflates implementation and algorithm; authors cite Kriegel et al. 2016 on this.
Tie-handling trick loses the exact-MST guarantee, giving an approximate MST; effect said to be small after condensing, worst for high-dimensional kd/ball trees.
Inherently serial; no parallel version. No cover tree support, so scaling with dimension is limited.
Single machine (8GB laptop), scikit-learn 0.18.1; HDBSCAN k and m used in benchmarks not stated; benchmark speeds are dated.
DBSCAN comparison gives DBSCAN its best-matching parameters, which a user would not know a priori (authors note this).

terms.definition: max of the two points' core distances and their distance; core distance is the distance to the kth nearest neighbor
clustering finds natural subsets without necessarily assigning every point; partitioning assigns every point
sum over points of the range of lambda (1/epsilon) for which the point is in the cluster; flat clusters maximise total stability without overlap
child clusters with fewer than m points are spurious splits and their points fall out of the parent
